speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MACKENZIE KING STATEMENT CONCERNING EXPENDITURES IN CONNECTION WITH TRIP TO BERMUDA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of personal privilege. The press of yesterday and to-day in reporting the proceedings before the select standing committee investigating the Beauharnois project has in certain quarters placed its own interpretation upon the evidence which was given there. I have in my hand one publication bearing the following heading:
Beauharnois paid bills of ex-Premier King. Mackenzie King's jaunt to Bermuda with Senator financed by Beauharnois.
I just wish to say Mr. Speaker that no bills of mine were ever paid by Beauharnois. I
[Mr. Hanbury.l
had no connection whatever with Beauharnois in any way, with respect to any matter of travel or anything else, and also I did not make the trip to Bermuda with Senator Mc-Dougald, as one might infer by reading the headings of articles appearing in some newspapers of yesterday and to-day.
The statement upon which these articles are based is a voucher presented yesterday to the committee which reads as follows:
April 30, 1930.-Expenses of trip to Bermuda Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King and self, hotel Bermuda, $288.53. Fares Montreal to Bermuda and return, $395.04. Hotel, New York, $168.75. Total, $852.32.
If one were to read this voucher without reading the evidence given yesterday by Senator McDougald, there might be some justification for headings which would seek to place upon the matter the interpretation to which I have referred. Senator Mc-Dougald's evidence given yesterday however makes perfectly clear the facts that this voucher was one which was put in, if not by himself by some one connected with his office, that it should never have been put in, that it was not a correct statement of his expenses and that it was in fact wholly erroneous.
May I say that at Easter of last year I paid a visit to Bermuda. On the way through the city of Montreal I saw Senator McDougald. He came into my car for a moment and spoke to me there. I did not see him again until I arrived at Bermuda, and when I was leaving I found that Senator McDougald who had been there during part of my stay had in part settled the account of myself and Senator Haydon who accompanied me on the trip. Senator McDougald left Bermuda before I did, and I did not accompany him to New York. I saw him in New York. I stayed one night at the Ritz Carlton hotel. The senator himself was not in New York at the time; I had received word that he had reserved accommodation there for Senator Haydon and myself and we stayed that night in the hotel. On the following day Senator McDougald came to the hotel with his wife with whom he had been in Atlantic City, and took up the accommodation he had reserved for himself. Senator McDougald did not pay any expenses whatever of either Senator Haydon or myself for transportation from Ottawa to Bermuda either by land or water, nor did he pay any transportation whatever from Bermuda back to Ottawa. All he did was to pay, himself, some of the hotel expenses while he had been a guest with Senator Haydon and myself.

Privilege-Mr. Mackenzie King
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that any attempt to draw an inference from the fact that on an Easter vacation I went to Bermuda with another member of this parliament and was met there by a second member, and that this meant that in any way I was violating any matter of honour in any particular is an inference which cannot be drawn by anyone who has an honourable mind. My purpose in going to Bermuda was twofold: I had in mind first of all the need of some vacation at the Easter recess. As hon. members know, whoever is filling the office of Prime Minister in Canada when parliament is in session is on certain occasions very much in need of rest. I took very few vacations during the time I was Prime Minister, and last year when the house was having the Easter recess I visited Bermuda. The primary object in my mind in going to Bermuda was this: In the government we had been discussing the terms of what is known as the Dunning budget, under which it was proposed to increase the duties against the United . States on fruit and vegetables. It was further proposed to reduce the duties under the British preference, and I was anxious to ascertain whether in the event of fruits and vegetables being made free from Bermuda and the West Indies there was a possibility or a probability of Bermuda and the other islands reciprocating by lowering their duties on some of our commodities going into those countries. While in Bermuda I discussed this matter with several members of the legislature and received assurances that if Canada did lower her duties on fruits and vegetables they were quite sure the islands would respond speedily by reducing some duties in our favour. That step was taken very shortly after our return.
Had I been thinking of enjoying a vacation at the expense of anyone I might, I suppose, have interpreted the trip-had I so desired to do, or been of a mind to do that kind of thing-as one which was associated with public business. I was so scrupulously careful however to avoid anything which might even remotely resemble anything of the kind that I regarded the entire trip to Bermuda and return as a vacation, and not a cent of money was charged against any account of the government or of any other organization or corporation of which I have any knowledge whatever.
I just wish to make that statement, Mr. Speaker, repeating that I am in no way responsible for any bills that may have been submitted by Senator McDougald to the Beauhamois company. I had no knowledge
whatever of any such bills being submitted. I was horrified when I learned of the voucher that was presented before the committee; so much so that I immediately went to the Prime Minister and told him of my trip to Bermuda and the circumstances surrounding it. I fail yet to understand how any such voucher could possibly have been put in. I want the house to understand that any bills that were put into the Beauharnois company were not put in with my knowledge or with my consent; they were not put in by me or on my account, but were put in by Senator McDougald with respect to expenses which he himself had incurred.
May I add this further fact, which possibly I should have mentioned at the outset: That I had no knowledge that Senator McDougald had settled the hotel account at Bermuda until I was about to pay my bill, when the clerk informed me that the Senator, before leaving, had paid the account-for the most, part, not in its entirety-and that therefore there was no further charge to be made in connection therewith.

PRIVILEGE-Mr. VENIOT
On the orders of the day:

Before
going on with the orders of the day I rise to a question of privilege, which includes the privileges of parliament as well as the personal privileges of myself as a member of
parliament. On April 27 an order was passed for the production of papers in the case of Nordin v. the King. These papers were asked for by the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. White):	Seeing that the papers were
not produced, and being interested in obtaining the information contained in that file, on June 5 I took up the matter. The Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) then informed me that he would look into the matter. I believe this was on a Friday, and the following Monday or Tuesday he informed me that he had discovered that the wrong file had been looked at, and that later on the matter would be attended to.
Up to the present time these papers have not been produced. Since this file has to do entirely with the Department of Railways and Oanals, and since it is not the practice for the Secretary of State to produce papers except when they come from more than one department, I would now ask the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion) if there is any reason why these papers have not been produced, or if there is any reason why they should not be produced. When the minister gives that reason I should like to have the opportunity, on a question of privilege, of discussing the matter further.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways and Canals):
speechtext:
It is not in the least
the fault of the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) that these papers have not been produced. It is my own fault, or perhaps I should say it is to my credit that this has not been done, and the reason is this: The production of these papers is being asked for -and in saying this I am in no way reflecting upon my hon. friend-for the purpose of permitting someone who wishes to sue the government to get certain information from our files. Since our department does not believe that the people who are going to sue the government in this matter have a just case, it was and is my opinion that it is not the duty of the government or of any department of the government to submit files for the purpose of enlightening some legal firm who may desire to secure information from those files which will assist them in preparing their case. I am not saying this in any spirit of criticism with regard to my hon. friend, because an hon. member on this side of the hoi^e moved for the production of those papers, I believe, on a previous occasion. The resolution slipped through; I do not remember when it was passed and I do not remember knowing anything about it when it did go through, but at any rate it was passed.
Privilege-Mr. Veniot
On April 22.

I do not question that,
nor do I question my hon. friend's intentions at all. But I repeat that I cannot see why, in a case like this, the government should be in a different position from a private corporation, which certainly would not show its files to an opposing group who might desire to sue them. I think the government, in the public interest, should refuse to permit the file to be brought down.
Is that the infallible justice of the crown?
My hon. friend had better stick to free trade.

In discussing this matter
further permit me to direct the attention of the Minister of Railways and Canals first to the fact that an order of this house has been passed directing that these papers be produced, and the minister himself has no right to refuse to obey the orders of this house. Further, let me refer to standing order 51, which has to do with the papers that may be produced. Among others I find:
.... for returns of petitions of right ....
There has been a petition of right in this case, and I claim that as a member of this house I am entitled to have that petition of right brought down and action taken upon it. Then the standing order goes on:
.... and cases before supreme and exchequer courts. . . .
Let me go further:	It is a principle of
British justice that the crown shall do nothing to prevent a citizen of the country from obtaining justice, and that the crown should in every way facilitate the obtaining of that justice. We have rulings on that point even from the privy council, and that is well laid down.

Canada is so obviously within the knowledge of the hon. gentleman, as it is within mine, that that particular question seemed to be of no special importance. The act was passed, it received the assent of the Governor General, and that assent was reported to the house. The other questions involve communications with the Dominion government office in London, the ascertaining from the government of Switzerland what other countries are adhering to the Rome convention, and other questions which can be answered only by information obtained from abroad. Arising out of the remarks of the Secretary of State, I might, if I so desired, raise a question of privilege. I should have reason to resent the inference which may be drawn from his observation that I ought to be aware that the Copyright Act is in force in Canada. I am aware that it is in force, but I am not aware that the revised convention of Berne, to which we were supposed to adhere, and which is an appendix to that law, is in force in Canada. I should be very much interested if the hon. gentleman would say whether Canada is at present an adherent of the Rome convention, and whether the appendix to the act is in force or not. As a matter of fact, I doubt whether he himself knows.

There is no doubt that the government of Canada requested His Majesty to adhere, on behalf of Canada, to the Rome convention, some days before the expiry of the time fixed-I think it was June 30. The hon. gentleman asks what other nations have adhered, and we must obtain that information from abroad. It has not yet been obtained. With regard to the Rome convention being in force in Canada, this Dominion has adhered to that convention and this parliament has enacted the legislation which has been deemed necessary in order that the provisions of the convention may be enforced in the courts of Canada.

I assume that every hon. member has in the meantime probably read the agreement and is familiar with its provisions, but I will state briefly the general principles that governed in connection with its negotiation and execution.
It was realized that Australia produces a large number of commodities which are not produced in Canada and which Canada must import from some other part of the world. It was realized that Canada produces commodities which Australia imports and buys from other parts of the world. The agreement endeavours to provide and does in fact provide that such commodities as Canada produces and Australia requires shall find a favoured market in Australia and that such commodities as Australia produces and Canada requires shall find a favoured place in Canadian markets. That is the first great principle which governed in the negotiation of this agreement.
In the second place it has been provided that where goods or commodities are produced in Australia which would compete with Canadian goods or commodities, then there must be such tariff provisions as will ensure fair competition in Canada to the goods from Australia, and equally, goods produced in Canada which come into competition with Australian goods in Australia shall, by virtue of the tariff provisions, enter into fair competition in Australia with Australian goods.
I need hardly say that the effort made to negotiate this measure of reciprocity in trade between the two countries is further predicated upon the thought that the agreement must be of mutual advantage to both coun-
[DOT]1036

Australian Trade Agreement
tries. If the principles to which I have alluded are applied, obviously they will be of mutual advantage to the communities affected. Unless a trade agreement benefits both countries it is not usually of very much use, but we believe and the Australians believe that the application of these principles will be mutually advantageous to Australia and to Canada.
In 1925 a trade agreement was negotiated with Australia. Under the terms of that agreement Canada received British preferential treatment with respect to four items out of a total tariff of 430 items; under the new agreement Canada will receive British preferential treatment on 415 items out of a total of 433. Under the agreement of 1925, Canada received intermediate tariff treatment on four items; under the agreement now before the house, Canada will receive intermediate tariff treatment on six items. Under the agreement of 1925, the general tariff applied on exportations to Australia in the case of 422 items; under the new agreement, the general tariff applies only to twelve items. In other words, while there were 430 items in the tariff of 1925 and 433 items in the tariff of 1931, we receive preferential treatment with respect to 421 items while the general tariff applies only to twelve items. Under the agreement of 1925, the general tariff applied to 422 items while preferential treatment was given only to eight items. The new agreement indicates a distinct advance and I believe it will commend itself to the judgment of this house and of the country. We are sure that this agreement will expand the trade of Canada in the east as well as in the west and it will afford an opportunity for raw materials as well as for finished products.
If on first perusal there are those who believe that too favourable treatment has been extended to Australia, in the main it will be because they have not perused the agreement with care. No agreement can be of service which does not afford a fair opportunity to Australia, such as we ourselves seek in her markets. I need hardly point out that I received a communication from a friend of mine saying that he was very much alarmed with regard to meats. He said that it was a serious situation, because Australia could produce meat readily. I replied that under the present agreement the rate was one-half cent a pound, but in order to maintain the principle to which I alluded in my earlier remarks, we have provided a duty of three cents a pound, which is four times what it was before with respect to some items, and six times what it was with respect to others.
i'Mr. Bennett.]
With regard to eggs which were on the free list under the old agreement, we have not imported a dollar's worth of eggs since the agreement was made. Now we have provided that there shall be a duty of two cents a dozen against importations except during certain months of the year. We have also made provision with respect to fruits and other products of the tropical sections of Australia. We have provided a market for the lumber of this country. I say frankly, as I have so often said, I have always found it difficult to understand how any bargain could be made with Australia that did not make some provision for a preference being given to Canadian lumber in that commonwealth; but such was not the case. In this agreement, however, that provision is made.
I shall not go through the various items in the schedule to the agreement, because they will be dealt with in committee. The bill follows the course that has usually been adopted in such cases and ratifies and confirms the agreement as it stands. It provides that if there is any inconsistency between the agreement and the act which ratifies it, and any other laws, the provisions of the act and the agreement shall prevail. Lastly, it provides that the agreement shall come into force on a day agreed upon by the government of Australia and the government of Canada as a result of a proclamation to be made by the governor in council in that commonwealth and in Canada as well.
I do not think there is anything I can usefully add to what I have said as to the principles that have governed in the negotiation of the agreement. How they have been applied will be Observed as the house proceeds to consider the agreement in committee. I believe it is such an agreement as will commend itself to the thoughtful and considered judgment of the house. I am already advised that it -commends itself to the business community of Canada in every part of it, and although at first sight there were some items that invited criticism, on further investigation it was found that there was no warrant for such criticism, nothing but a frank recognition of two great principles which have governed the negotiation of an agreement between two British commonwealths. We believe also this is a step towards the development of empire trade on sound lines, not of endeavouring to get without giving nor of giving without getting, but of giving and getting. That principle has governed and it will be the ultimate principle that will govern and prevail with respect to the development of trade throughout the British Empire.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING ('Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
The bill, the

Australian Trade Agreement
second reading of which has just been moved by my right hon. friend, is one which creates -a new trade agreement with Australia. Inasmuch as the previous Liberal administration was the first to initiate a trade agreement with that particular sister dominion, we naturally take no exception to the underlying principle of the bill. The fact that this bill also recognizes the importance of reciprocal treatment in trade between different parts of the British Empire makes it only the more commendable in principle to those of us on this side of the house, for it will be remembered that it was a Liberal administration which was the first to introduce the principle of the British preference, and the first to make it an empire preference.
My right hon. friend spoke of some things being produced in Australia which could not be produced in Canada, and some things being produced in Canada which could not be produced in Australia. He said that the trade treaty would make possible the exchange of those particular commodities. In speaking on the budget I pointed out that I believed it would be possible for the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) in negotiating a treaty in accordance with the principles which he had laid down as those which should govern in trade agreements, to go further in negotiating a treaty with Australia, than would be the case with any other of the sister dominions, and very much further than would be possible in a trade agreement with the mother country, and this for the particular reason that Australia being a tropical or quasi-tropical country and Canada being in the temperate zone, there would, in the nature of things, be more in the way of what might be described as an absolute advantage in production on the part of each one of these countries in its relation to the other with respect to certain commodities than would be the case as regards Canada in relation to any other country. Therefore I am not surprised that my right hon. friend has started with Australia in his effort to make the further trade treaties which he has in mind.
But may I say that when he provides in this treaty for trading to any extent beyond the point of absolute advantage, he runs counter to the principle which he laid down as being fundamental in trade treaties, namely, that nothing should be imported into Canada which can be produced or manufactured in Canada. I think those are the words which the Prime Minister himself on different occasions has given to the house as setting forth his policy in trade matters. He has said repeatedly, that it is our business to see that what can be produced or manufactured in Canada should
not be permitted to be imported from other countries. There is in this treaty a considerable departure from that principle, and, indeed, if there had not been, I question very much whether any treaty could have been made.
My right hon. friend spoke of mutual advantage. I should like to ask him if he can tell me of any exchange that is ever made between individuals that is not believed to be in the nature of mutual advantage. Mutual advantage is of the very essence of exchange. One person parts with what he possesses either in the form of goods or money for something which he .wishes to get in exchange and which will mean more to him as a consequence of his exchange than to retain the commodity or the money which he exchanges for it. What is true on one side of a bargain is equally true on the other. International trade is nothing more than trade between individuals at large so far as one nation is concerned with individuals at large so far as another nation is concerned. All trade is, as I have already said, in the nature of an exchange for purposes of mutual advantage. It is there that there is a real difference between my right hon. friend and those who follow the doctrines which he lays down, and those of us on this side who believe that with greater freedom of trade there will be in the end a greater national development.
My right hon. friend has said that he assumes we have all had an opportunity to study this treaty and that we can discuss its items in committee. The criticism which I have to direct most strongly against the government with respect to this measure is that they have waited until the close of the session, at a time when there are so many important measures before the house, to bring in this particular treaty. There has really been no opportunity at all in the time that we have had since the agreement was laid upon the table, to consider its features in any proper manner. My right hon. friend speaks of four hundred and some odd items in one relationship and some four hundred odd or more in another. The value of the agreement can be estimated only when we discover the true significance of the different items. It may well be that some of them will indicate so far as Canada is concerned a possibility of more advantageous trade with Australia than that which existed before. Unless however we know in all items what the Australian tariff is in comparison with our own tariff we cannot make the comparisons necessary to draw proper deductions. That opportunity hon. members of this house have not had. In speaking the other day my right hon. friend said that he himself could not

Australian Trade Agreement
give the house a statement as to what the Australian tariff actually was, that it was being constantly changed, and that it was being changed at this very time. I have no doubt that some of those alterations will very materially affect the value of the agreement. My right hon. friend has said under the old treaty a very small number of commodities, relatively, were given a preference, while under the proposed treaty a very large number would be given a preference. Whether that preference means anything or not will depend upon the preferential tariff which exists in Australia, and whether it will mean more or less to Australia than to Canada will depend upon whether the preference given under the tariff in Canada is greater or less than that given by Australia to Canada. The Minister of Finance will not deny that the preference which under her customs tariff Canada gives Australia is very much greater than that which Australia gives to Canada under her customs tariff. So far as there is an advantage of one country over another in the exchange of goods or commodities, in this instance the advantage lies with Australia rather than with Canada, May I state further that the height of the preferential tariff in Australia is I believe in many cases quite as great if not greater than that of our general tariff,-certainly as great as that of our general tariff as it existed before it was amended in the special and present sessions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Perhaps the right hon.
gentleman does not understand; on 400 odd items they extend to us the British preference.

Exactly. On 400 items there is the British preference, but the British preference in Australia differs from the British preference in Canada. That is the point I am trying to make. Whereas in Canada the tariff rates governing our British preference might be rated-and I speak without reference to any particular item -at something like 20 per cent, that is to say the duty might average 20 per cent, in Australia in all probability it will be 40 per cent.
Much more than that.

My hon. friend the former Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler) says it will be much more than that. In other words the preference granted by Australia when it is examined carefully so as correctly to understand this measure, really does not amount to very much because even the preferential tariff is already virtually prohibitive.
In Australia they have done what my right hon. friend is attempting to do in Canada. They have really made it impossible, even
[Mr Mackenzie King.]
under the British preference, for commodities produced or manufactured outside of Australia to be imported into that country. What the result of that policy has been one has but to study the conditions in Australia to learn. Certainly it would scarcely be proper to refer here to a condition in any other country, particularly that of a sister dominion. The general position of Australia as contrasted with that of Canada is, however, well enough known to enable us to see for ourselves that the policy of making the tariff, both general and preferential, so high that most commodities cannot enter a country thereby restricting trade in large part, is not a policy which in the long run makes for good. In connection with the Australian tariff there is a 50 per cent-is it a surtax?
Yes.

Yes, a surtax, in addition to the tariff which has to be met, that makes the importation of most commodities from this country into Australia almost prohibitive.
There is another circumstance which is most important and which I believe in large part will determine the fate of the proposed treaty, namely, the position of the currency in Australia at the present time. As is generally known the currency of that country is considerably depreciated, and in estimating how far it will be possible for Australia to purchase commodities from Canada we have to take into account the position of the credit and currency of that country. Again I say that I do not think it would be proper to reflect upon conditions in a sister dominion. I mention this matter however simply as one of the outstanding economic facts which has to be considered in discerning the merits of an agreement of this kind. It may be that if the government hopes to derive any real benefit from this proposed trade agreement it will have to extend credits to Australia to enable that country to purchase goods from Canada. If we are to judge from previous experience in giving credits to other countries to enable them to purchase our commodities, I submit that great care would have to be exercised before such a step should again be taken.
My right hon. friend has referred to the lumber industry and has said he could scarcely imagine an effective trade agreement with Australia which did not include a considerable opportunity for the export of lumber from Canada. He frequently speaks of the depletion of our natural resources as one of the terrible results of trade. Lumber is a manufactured natural resource. Following him in his own view I see somewhat of a contradiction in an arrangement which enables us to

part more rapidly than we ought with the great natural resources of our forests.

I cannot see that the depreciated currency of Australia is going to help the Canadian who has commodities to sell to Australia. That is the point I was making. It will take much more depreciated currency to buy a commodity in terms of dollars than it would require of a currency that was not depreciated.

Is it not as broad as
it is long, is there not that much more of the currency in circulation?

If currency
was just a nominal affair and we could put whatever denomination we liked on our values, my hon. friend's argument would be correct; but my view is that currency is a measure of value and a medium of exchange, and so far as it is a medium of exchange its real worth in international relations is just what a given quantity will buy in terms of commodities.

Mr. Speaker, so far as I could hear the statement of the Prime Minister, I feel that very little exception, if any, could be taken to the basis which he says underlies the negotiations for this treaty. The number of items which have received the benefit of the Australian British preferential tariff is not necessarily any indication of the real worth of the treaty. I believe that on many items the Australian British preferential tariff is so high that we cannot expect to sell any goods to Australia.
I have not had time to secure the Australian tariff and go into the details of these different items, and I think we must wait until the committee stage is reached before we can determine how mqch value the British preferential tariff on any of these items will be to Canada. I hope the agreement will be just as beneficial to Canada as the Prime Minister seems to expect, but I think there is a tendency to overrate the advantages likely to accrue to Canada. In this connection I desire to quote from the Einancial Post of the 18th instant. I am citing this paper because it is considered a very reliable financial journal. Dealing with the new trade treaty with Australia it says:
The Australian treaty opens up, for the first time, substantial opportunities for many classes of Canadian producers in Australia. Canadians, in many items, are put on a parity with British manufacturers. Canada has a geographical advantage in relation to Australia which will be of help in some lines, unimportant in others.
Yet too much must not be expected of the treaty at the moment. Australian purchasing power is at a low ebb; Australian exchange 
is subject to a large discount. This penalizes importers by 30 per cent and gives to Australian exporters a corresponding advantage.
That is the point I want to emphasize for the moment, particularly the concluding words:
This penalizes importers by 30 per cent and gives to Australian exporters a corresponding advantage.
That corresponding advantage will amount to 30 per cent. Looking at schedule A of the treaty for a moment I find the first item mentioned there, meat, fresh, namely: (a) beef and veal, 3 cents per pound.
Assuming for the sake of argument these meats would be worth on the average 10 cents a pound when imported into Canada, the premium which the Australian exporter would receive would amount to 3 cents a pound, which would be equivalent to the duty that we have placed against beef and veal coming from Australia. That is putting us on a free trade basis so far as those two meats are concerned. On (b) lamb and mutton, the duty is 3 cents per pound. Lamb and mutton, I think, would have a slightly higher value than 10 cents a pound. But assuming for the moment that the value would be only 10 cents a pound, the exporter frqm Australia would have a premium of 3 cents a pound on the present rates of exchange The next item on the schedule is canned meats, poultry or game; extracts of meats and fluid beef, not medicated, IS per cent ad valorem. Clearly the 30 per cent advantage enjoyed by the Australian exporter will give him a sufficient premium to more than pay the tariff; it is practically double the tariff placed against canned meats. Coming down to eggs in the shell, they are free during the months of January and February; British preferential tariff during the other months of the year. That rate, I believe, is 2 cents a dozen. If these eggs have a value of even 10 cents a dozen when landed in Canada, the premium enjoyed by the Australian exporter will be 3 cents a dozen, which is more than the tariff placed against the Australian exporter to Canada. Then take cheese, item No. 17, on which the duty is 1 cent per pound. I suppose cheese should be worth at least 10 cents per pound wholesale, so the premium which the Australian exporter would enjoy would be 3 cents per pound, while our tariff is only 1 cent per pound. Then we come to butter, which is a very controversial item. Butter carries a duty of 5 cents per pound. I take it for granted that butter coming from Australia would be worth at least 20

cents a pound, so the premium of 30 per cent enjoyed by the Australian exporter would be 6 cents a pound, which would more than pay the duty.

I know many members of the house think the advantage enjoyed by the Australian exporter is a myth, and for their benefit I should like to quote very briefly from a speech delivered in this house in 1922 by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) in dealing with the budget of that year. The minister was referring to the question of depreciated currency and was urging upon the then Minister of Finance the necessity for placing a special duty on goods coming from countries whose currency had depreciated by more than 50 per cent. Of course the Australian currency is only depreciated at this moment by about 30 per cent.
No, 24 per cent.

The last figure I saw was
30 per cent, but whether it is 24 per cent or 30 per cent the same principle applies. I quote from the remarks of the Minister of Trade and Commerce as they appear in Hansard for June 8, 1922, at page 2642:
Now, I come to the next point, and that is the depreciated currency clause passed in amendment to the Customs Act last year. It is not necessary for me to go into the details of what it was; it was in effect simply this: That in any country where the currency had depreciated below a point of 50 per cent of par, the valuation for duty purposes upon goods imported from that country should be figured at a rate not less than 50 per cent.
Then he went on to deal with the German situation and to show that the tariff was very inadequate. Later on he referred to a statement made by the then member for West York, Sir Henry Drayton, as follows:
.... let me refer to a statement made by the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton), that this constituted free trade with Germany. I want to say to the house that it does not constitute free trade with Germany; it constitutes paying a premium on German imports.
I agree with what the hon. member said at that time. Then he went on to quote authorities to prove that this really was paying a premium. I do not want to take up too much of the time of the house, so I am only quoting very briefly from the remarks of the minister at that time. He went on to quote Doctor Melchior, a very prominent German economist, from an article which had appeared in the Manchester Guardian a short time previously, as follows:
The international value of the mark has a natural connection with its purchasing power in Germany,_ which in turn depends on inflation. The internal purchasing power of the mark .... is at present (April, 1922), between two and three times its international value. . . .
Then the minister said:
I want the house to follow very closely these last few words:
And he concluded the quotation from Doctor Melchior:
The falling currency has, it is true, brought apparent prosperity to German industry by means of a premium on exports-
Then the minister proceeded to quote further:
-which at the same time cripples the industries of the competing countries.
Doctor Melchior is an outstanding German economist who was very familiar with the German situation. There is no question but that he stated the case correctly; I am stating it correctly to-day, and the Financial Post is stating it correctly when it says the present rate which has to be paid in Australia for foreign exchange is creating a premium on the exports of that country which at the same time is crippling the industries of competing countries. Then the minister proceeded:
This is not my statement; this is not the statement of some wild-eyed, prejudiced person seeking vengeance on Germany; this is the statement of the highest economic authority in Germany who was at Versailles, who was the head of their economic agents and experts, and who has been at the head of almost every one of their conferences. Let me emphasize the words of Doctor Melchior: "Which at the same time cripples the industries of competing countries."
Then the minister went on to give some very good figures showing how impossible it

Now, this is what I want to emphasize. The Canadian manufacturer to-day is manufacturing at a lower cost and under-selling both the British and the American manufacturer of this particular article.
He was referring to some kind of knife, and I want to direct attention to these words:
Why should we ask him, however, to compete with such utterly unfair competition as that to which I have referred with this depreciated currency?
I am not suggesting for a moment that the depreciated currency of Australia to-day compares at all with the depreciated currency of Germany in 1922, but I say that the same principle is involved when we have to compete with goods coming from Australia. Just on that point I should like to quote from an unquestioned authority in regard to this matter, in order to prove that the Australian exporter enjoys a premium. A week or two ago we had before the agricultural committee Mr. Richardson, a very prominent grain exporter of western Canada and a member of one of the oldest grain firms in Canada. He was asked the following question:
Mr. Campbell: Would you suggest, then, that if the Canadian currency were depreciated to the extent that the Australian is, that is if the world's exchange were against us, would it put the Canadian farmer in the preferred position?
Mr. Richardson:	If our exchange were
depreciated, our wheat would be higher by probably 30 per cent.
A little later I asked Mr. Richardson this question:
Mr. Coote: Just to clear up that point, Mr. Richardson, is it not a fact that Australia has largely taken the oriental market from us on account of their exchange situation?
Mr. Richardson: Undoubtedly.

Mr. Richardson: Undoubtedly.

I want to wait until we have heard all the items discussed in committee so that we may see their true significance, but I do suggest that here is good evidence of the beneficial results which would come to Canada if we would suspend the redemption of our notes in gold', as was done during the war. No doubt our currency would depreciate to some extent; I would not predict just how far it might go, but the value of our dollar should be allowed to depend upon our trade balance and not upon the gold standard. If that were done there is

no doubt that the price of our wheat would be advanced by 15 cents a bushel without cost to the government of this country, while the debts of all the producers in Canada would be materially lessened.
I do not wish to take up more time in dealing with this point, but I should like to emphasize that it will be difficult Bor us to get any advantage from this Australian treaty unless our currency is somewhere near par with Australia's. If we would allow our currency to depreciate to the point to which the Australian currency has depreciated, so that we might be on a level with that Dominion, we could sell her more goods and at the same time secure a distinct advantage when we came to export our commodities to any country in the world1. I hope that before the treaty is in force very long the government will see the wisdom of putting us on a parity with Australia in the matter of currency. Let us put a little more money into circulation even if our dollar does depreciate somewhat, so that we may enjoy the same advantage that Australia now enjoys in the markets of the world. Wheat is Canada's greatest item of export. We cannot export any to Australia, that dominion and the Argentine being our greatest competitors, apart, possibly, from Russia. Australia is taking the oriental market from us, according to Mr. Richardson, and the Argentine is largely taking away the European market. There is only one way to prevent them from taking those markets away from us and that is to sell wheat at a ruinously low price. Mr. Speaker, I wish to deal with the matter now before the house from the point of view oi the province of British Columbia. Necessarily, the present agreement is a compromise. I believe it will materially benefit the fidhing, lumbering and newsprint industries in British Columbia. I regret only the fact that the coal industry of that province could not have received the same beneficent treatment. I might say that while the press of British Columbia is largely Conservative all papers have struck a very pleased note concerning the completion of this treaty. I think it is a very serious matter indeed, and I am afraid it will work out in this way:	The idea was
that if there were one special article in connection with which some grievance arose, such as butter in the case of the New Zealand agreement, we would not have to cancel the whole agreement but could strike out the preference on that particular article without prejudice to the rest of the agreement. Once you did away with the preference on butter you could have torn up the whole agreement, as far as New Zealand was concerned, and if we had not cancelled it no doubt New Zealand would have done so. Even supposing that were not so and you took one article and put it under the general tariff; later on you took another article and did the same thing, and how long would it be before the other party to the treaty would say, "This is not good enough; if you are going to pick out our best commodities one by one we will have to do the same thing, and there will be no treaty left." I believe that may be the way it will work out.

For years past I have listened to the Conservative party stressing the need not so much for dumping clauses, since we always had a technical dumping clause, but for what we might call the safeguards which rendered it possible to impose the dumping duty. The Conservative party demanded those safeguards from time to time very vigorously, and last September we saw those clauses enacted. I voted for them, believing they were required, but I rather regret my action after having seen how readily, how easily and above all how secretly it can be applied. There is no publicity at all; it simply appears in the Gazette, and how many of us take the Gazette? When you find your goods hung up at the border there is not much time left in which to look up the Gazette, or perhaps after having contracted for goods in the old country you find that the dumping duty is applied. It is not such a nice arrangement as I thought it would be.
Be that as it may, it is the settled policy of the Conservative party to have these safeguards, and we have them. Now, at a time and under conditions when, if ever, they would be most useful and most required, they have been taken away absolutely; we have legislated ourselves out of our rights. There was never such a thing done before; at least we always had the frame-work for a dumping duty, but now we are not going to be allowed to employ it under this treaty. I am afraid it will work very much against our interests. We know that the Australians are always changing their tariffs; they are changing them at the present time and they may do so at any time in the future. While, perhaps under a gentleman's agreement, the dumping duty might never be put in operation, it is a wonderful safeguard to have in the background. It was the means of remedying the butter situation; Australian butter would have been rushed in here but for the fact that we were able to keep it out through the dumping duty. It was bonused under the Paterson scheme, although I do not think it was quite as much as my hon. friend from North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) has said, because there was a 15 per cent restriction. At any rate, we took advantage of the dumping duty, having regard to the Paterson scheme, to stop Australian butter coming into this country.
As my hon. friend from North Waterloo has said, under the old treaty the Australian butter exporter had to pay a total of 7 cents. Supposing he sends a pound of butter to Vancouver which is sold in the open market
for 30 cents per pound in competition with British Columbia butter. Under the old treaty the Australian would have received 23 cents, and that difference was sufficient to stop the importation. Under the new duty he will get 30 cents less 5 cents duty, and in addition he has the advantage of a depreciated currency which at 30 per cent would be 8 cents, so his pound of butter would realize him 33 cents as against only 30 cents to the British Columbia man. I know my hon. friend will say 30 per cent is an excessive statement of the fluctuation of Australian currency, but it was 35 per cent a few weeks ago and may be 36 per cent again, so I think 30 per cent is not excessive. If the currency improves, of course, that condition will not obtain, but we have no knowledge and in fact very little hope, I think, that the Australian currency situation will improve in the near future.

Not if it is impossible to manufacture the article under certain conditions. The hon. gentleman is not familiar with the situation. He does not know that there are remote localities and other conditions where it would not be profitable to convert the timber into newsprint. But they can make sulphite which is afterwards taken to the factory and manufactured into newsprint. Surely, however, the hon. gentleman will not suggest that the pulp and sulphite industry Should have been, to put it mildly, neglected. Surely he does not suggest that they should be passed over and ignored.
Has my hon. friend received complaints from the pulp industry of British Columbia on the subject?

Not since the treaty was
passed, but I received an urgent request that I should endeavour to have some consideration given pulp and sulphite. I was asked to see whether the industry could not be given some of the benefits Of the treaty.
Did my hon. friend try?
Yes, I tried.
I don't remember.
Yes, I tried.
I do not remember having heard from him at all-not a single word. I never heard from him.
No?
Not on that subject.
He has heard from me often.
The hon. gentleman said he tried to get it in the treaty. He never came near us, nor asked us, nor suggested it to us.
Am I not trying to get it in now?
After the treaty has been signed?
The treaty has been signed, it is true-

Signed by both parties
and delivered.
It has been signed but not ratified; and it is not law and is not binding until it is ratified.
Will you reject the treaty to get it in or take the treaty without it?

That is the same question: the hon. gentleman is trying to trick me into a false position. He asks, "Will you forego the great advantages of the treaty because certain things are not included in it?" Well, two blacks do not make a white, nor do two wrongs make a right. I am saying that the treaty is of great advantage to a large number of interests in British Columbia, but I am pointing out that certain interests have been ignored.
The hon. gentleman made no representations on their behalf during the last nine months while the treaty has been under negotiation.

My time is drawing to a close and I must finish what I have to say. As regards eggs, I have already put on record the opinion of those who are best calculated to know what the results will be. As regards butter, I fear that the market will again be flooded because of the absence of the dumping clause. I regret that the dumping clause has been abandoned in this regard1. That is one outstanding mistake in the treaty. Notwithstanding this, however, and on the principle of the greatest good to the greatest number, I may answer my hon. friend's challenge whether I will vote for the treaty by assuring him that I will. It will be of considerable advantage to a great many people in British Columbia, and on that principle, of the greatest good to the greatest number, I will support it. But that does not and will not prevent me from pointing out wherein I think it might have been improved upon, without any very great loss to us with regard to the interests I have indicated.

Don't be wasting our time.

My hon. friend is very fond of interrupting. If he will get up on his hind legs and address the committee in whatever language is familiar to him, I will listen to him. If he is not getting the amount of hay and oats-or perhaps thistles-he thinks he is entitled to, let him go to his keeper.
If I cannot make a better speech than that the proper thing for me to do is to keep my seat.

I do not intend to detain the house, but I wish to refer to two items in particular in the treaty, namely, lumber and newsprint. In passing, may I comment briefly on the observations of my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) with reference to newsprint paper versus pulp and sulphite. That, I think, was the way in which he referred to these two items. There are three kinds of pulp manufactured in Canada, sulphite, sulphate and groundwood. Sulphite and ground-wood are used in the manufacture of newsprint in the proportion of approximately 84 or 85 per cent of groundwood to 15 or 16 per cent of sulphite. If you make provision by which you are enabled to export 15 or 16 tons of sulphite and 84 or 85 tons of groundwood pulp, you simply take away from yourself a market for 100 tons of newsprint. From the standpoint of British Columbia, where both pulp and paper is manufactured, if we can export newsprint we provide a market for an equal tonnage of sulphite and groundwood pulp. It is better for the country to manufacture the paper to the highest possible degree and give employment to an additional number of Canadian workmen. Although I have not the information before me, I believe the same thing would apply to sulphate which is used in the manufacture of kraft paper. When my hon. friend says that sulphite and pulp-I presume he is referring to groundwood-cannot be manufactured into newsprint, I believe he must be mistaken.
I did not say that.
I understood the hon. gentleman to say that the sulphite and pulp industries were being penalized because conditions were such that those commodities could not be converted into newsprint.
Oh, no.
The wood itself is the raw product.
My hon. friend has misunderstood me. I said that it could not in many instances be manufactured profitably immediately into newsprint.

There is no doubt a
paper mill cannot be erected wherever a pulp mill is in operation, but it is equally true that sulphite and groundwood are the semi-raw products from which newsprint is manufactured, and if you provide a market for newsprint you provide a market for sulphite and groundwood, which in turn provides more employment for Canadian workmen.
Every million feet of lumber which is exported from any part of Canada will provide more employment than an equal value of any other product produced in Canada. The provision of a market for an additional 100,006,000 feet of lumber would provide, directly or indirectly, for 50,000 Canadians. It would provide directly for 7,500 people, then there would *be in addition all that is involved in the maintenance of 7,500 people, and the purchase of equipment, provisions and so on, which would involve an amount almost equal to the sum paid in wages in the industry.
My hon. friend was stressing the point that pulp and sulphite should not be exported but should be manufactured into newsprint, but he says now that the raw lumber should be exported.

That argument does
not hold. A hundred different articles can be manufactured from faw lumber. The principal use to which raw lumber is put is the erection of all kinds of buildings. Does my hon. friend suggest thart. we should limit the export of lumber until we can provide the means by which we would erect the buildings, and export them as such? Ground-wood and sulphite are the raw products for newsprint, and when we export newsprint we are exporting groundwood and sulphite. Does my hon. friend contend that we should limit the export of lumber because we do not manufacture the buildings for export? Lumber which goes into the manufacture of furniture is of an entirely different class. Some goes into the manufacture of doors, but that article is provided for in the treaty. The exporting of lumber would provide more work for Canadian people than a proportionate amount of any other commodity manufactured in this country.

This is unmanufactured
lumber.

To what does my
hon. friend refer as unmanufactured lumber?
Not manufactured.

If I understand this
bill it provides for all sizes of lumber.

Including logs.
Australian Trade Agreement

Yes, but how many
logs will be exported to Australia? I am not very familiar with the lumbering trade of British Columbia, but I do know that some of the largest saw mills in the country are located in that province. When a market is provided for the product of those mills the pressure will be relieved which is now being *exerted on the eastern market by the British Columbia trade. If there were no other provisions in the treaty than those covering the export of newsprint and lumber, the treaty would be well worth while. There is no other industry in Canada, not excluding wheat, in which unemployment has increased to a greater degree than in the lumbering and newsprint industry'.

Under the terms of the
old treaty, salmon, sturgeon and other canned fish were all on the same basis. Under the terms of the new treaty salmon receives a preference of three pence as compared with one and a half pence.

Mr. Speaker, I have noticed some
criticism of the Australian treaty, and I will venture tihe assertion that it is unlikely there ever will be a treaty which will not call for criticism from some branch of the community or some individuals interested. Speaking as I do for my constituency in British Columbia, I can only say frankly that I congratulate the government upon the treaty. In so doing I should like to associate, and I feel confident the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) would also associate with this treaty, those gentlemen from British Columbia who, about a year and a half ago, partly at the expense of tire British Columbia Lumber and Shingle Manufacturers' Association, assisted by the government of that province, went to Australia and New Zealand, their main purpose being that British Columbia lumber should be given a preference in those two dominions. The gentlemen to whom I refer are Mr. J. C. McDonald, Mr. J. G. Robson, bath of them from the city of New Westminster, and Mr. T. Gadd, of the city of Vancouver. All of these gentlemen are members of the British Columbia Lumber and Shingle Manufacturers' Association. As secretary of that group they took along with them Major Andrews, and it may be of some interest to members of the house to know that the Major Andrews to whom I refer is a son-in-law of the Premier of British Columbia, the Hon. Doctor Tolmie. They were given a great deal of encouragement by the governments and industrials of both Australia and New Zealand. Prior to their departure from Canada they had been in consultation with the then Minister of Trade and Commerce. After their return they arranged that Major Andrews, who had accompanied them on this trip, should reside permanently in Australia. It is only right that the efforts of all these gentlemen should be recognized in connection with this treaty.
Newsprint is to be an item on which Canada gets a preference in the markets of Australia. I would, however, point out to the house that Canada, or British Columbia-it is practically the same thing in this particular case-has been furnishing approximately one-third of the newsprint requirements of Australia. The other two-tliirds have been purchased from Great Britain. So that it is difficult to see wherein British Columbia is to get a preference over what has been in the past our chief competitor. Unquestionably, however, the preference has been increased to such an extent that there is little likelihood of other nations successfully competing for the newsprint market.
In respect to Australia's lumber requirements we have not been so fortunate. Canada has never been given a preference in connection with the lumber requirements of Australia. The total importation into Australia of lumber that could have been supplied by British Columbia-I refer chiefly to Douglas fir-was 212,000.000 feet in 1928. Of that Canada supplied only about 13 per cent. In 1929 we increased the percentage to some extent. Australia imported approximately 266,000,000 feet, but even so, less than 22 per cent was furnished from Canada, practically the whole of the remainder being obtained from Washington and Oregon, which compete directly' with British Columbia in furnishing Douglas fir, or, as it is known in many countries, Oregon pine. I am pleased to note that the treaty also includes redwood or cedar. Redwood is not grown in British Columbia, but cedar is. In the past I understand redwood from California has had a preference in Australia over British Columbia cedar. Now British Columbia cedar will have a preference over the redwood of California,

Australian Trade Agreement
and this should be a big advantage to the lumber interests of our province.
As regards canned salmon, we have in the past supplied approximately 70 per cent of the requirements of Australia. Therefore, from the standpoint of British Columbia we have a possible expansion of the newsprint supply; we have a possible expansion of 200 or 300 or 400 per cent in the quantity of lumber, and a possible increase of 50 per cent in the quantity of canned fish that can go from Canada to Australia. Consequently the treaty appeals to me as one that is worthy of the favourable consideration of the house.
Some criticism has been made in connection with our importation of eggs and butter. It is only reasonable to assume that if we can increase the production of newsprint, lumber and canned fish, the increase in the number of the employed will result in the consumption of a very large quantity of the surplus eggs that are now available. At the present time, however, eggs in Canada are on an export basis and so long as this condition continues I can see little disadvantage to the Canadian producer, whether eggs come into this country and force the sale of a larger quantity of his surplus outside Canada, or whether he sells his whole production inside or outside this country. So long as butter and eggs are on an export basis I can see very little injury to butter or egg production in Canada.
It has been stated as a ground of criticism that many items of the treaty are not such as will be exchanged between Canada and Australia. True, we may not exchange these commodities, but I can see no disadvantage in having them mentioned in the treaty. It is something like the cast iron pipe and cut flowers about which we heard so much a year or so ago.
The important question is not so much whether the exchange of commodities is to be to the advantage of Canada, but whether it will be possible for Canada to sell gobds to Australia at all. As was pointed out this afternoon by my leader, many of the duties, even under the British preference, are higher than our general tariff, and in addition to that they have a surtax of 50 per cent on many items. The latter, we are informed, is a temporary measure, but the fact remains that this surtax of 50 per cent does that much more to exclude the importation into Australia of goods from any country and makes it just that much more difficult for Canadian shippers to reach the consumer in Australia. In addition to the duty and the surtax, they have what is known as a general primage tax duty of 10
[Mr. HanburyJ
per cent, so that in many cases there is the surtax of 50 per cent, and in all cases the primage tax. That, however, is to my mind not the worst feature, because Australia has in the past, and will in the future purchase goods regardless of the height of her tariff.
What should concern us chiefly at this time is the inability of Australia to furnish money with which to purchase the commodities not only of Canada but of every countiy in the world. At the present time Australia is restricting the export of exchange. There are merchants in Canada who for some time past have been unable to transfer their credits from Australia to Canada, and I understand that condition exists to-day. Therefore Mr. Speaker, if we are to take advantage of the Australian treaty, if we are to furnish work for the lumbermen of British Columbia and other parts of Canada, for the paper mills and paper mill workers in British Columbia and other parts of Canada and, for the fishermen, we must make some provision whereby the goods they produce can be sold in Australia. Otherwise of what advantage would such a treaty be to this or any other country?
I suggest therefore, since each of these commodities entails a very high percentage of labour, that in view of the present economic and unemployment conditions the government could, if on no other grounds, justify an extension to Australia of a credit which could not be used outside of Canada. Until Australia is able to set her own house in order, until that country can permit the exportation of credits I see very little advantage in placing this treaty on the statute books. I suggest to the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that every effort should be made to establish credits in Canada so that the Canadian producer may sell his goods to Australia.
During the past few years the old Australian treaty was criticized in every part of Canada -yes, even in British Columbia. The basis of the criticism was that benefits accrued only to British 'Columbia. True, on account of her geographical position that province must reap the greater benefit of any treaty with Australia, New Zealand or any of the Pacific countries. In this particular treaty, however, I feel that the government of the day have provided some preference to producers of all classes of goods in all portions of Canada. Therefore I for one believe that an advance has been made, that a step forward has been taken, and I have no hesitation in saying that I for one heartily support the Australian treaty as submitted to this house

Mr. Speaker, I had intended to reserve my observations until the 6ID reached the committee stage, 'but after listening to a number of addresses this afternoon I have come to realize that at this stage perhaps a few words of explanation and some observations in reply to statements made by hon. members may be useful. If the house would consider that details can be given more fully in the committee stage my present remarks might tend to shorten the debate on the second reading.
During the long months which have elapsed since this treaty was originally under discussion there has been on the part of the representatives of Canada as well as of Australia nothing but the most earnest desire to cooperate in the production of an agreement which would be mutually advantageous. I think my colleagues will agree that throughout those months, which have entailed a great deal of labour there has been nothing but the most cordial good-will between the two dominions. Some difficulties have been experienced due largely to the great distances separating the two countries. Negotiations soncerning the treaty were commenced during the sessions of the economic conference, and at this point I wish to pay tribute to Mr. Moloney, who represented his country on the economic committees of the Imperial conference, upon the manner in which he approached the subject and the generous support he gave us in our efforts to bring the matter to a satisfactory conclusion.
Certain attitudes have been taken to-day towards the treaty, and I think a few words of explanation would serve to remove at least some of the apprehensions in the minds of hon. members opposite. I shall try to deal with hon. members in the order in which they have spoken, referring first to the observations of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). He referred to the fact that the Prime Minister Mr. Bennett) had said the agreement before us was a treaty of mutual advantage to both countries, and reiterated a homily on the mutuality of trade generally. I would invite the house to this thought however, that while certainly an exchange between two individuals must be or usually is of mutual advantage in that the two making the exchange are both pleased or satisfied, it is not correct to say that such is true between nations. The right hon. member laid it down as a definite and proven principle that because an exchange between individuals is mutually advantageous an exchange between
nations must necessarily be of the same order. Here is the difference. Trade between countries is trade between different individuals in each of the countries. For instance, if one country has no tariff at all-I use the extreme example in order to get the full force of the point-and the other has a high tariff, the individuals in the country with the low tariff could buy goods in the country with the high tariff and bring them in to the disadvantage of some of its own nationals. On the other hand it would be next to impossible, or certainly much more difficult, for individuals in the free trade country to ship their goods into the high tariff country to the injury of the individuals over there. It is conceivable therefore that a condition may exist between two countries where trade is not mutually advantageous. If however the two countries come together and examine the conditions of trade in each and the conditions controlling the interchange between the two, it is possible to iron out differences or at least to minimize the injury which might be done. That is precisely what we have tried to do in the agreement between Australia and Canada. It is clear that there are goods produced in both countries which are competitive; I might say that in some few instances they are highly competitive. On the other hand, there is a wide range of commodities where the one is the complement to the other. In this treaty we have sought to avoid the injury which keen competition from one of its commodities would do to the importing country. While we have sought to minimize, and indeed, almost eliminate, such a danger, on the other hand there is a wide range of exchange of goods that may be carried on without injury to either country, and that is what we have tried to facilitate.
Now, I was very sorry when I heard the right hon. gentleman offer criticisms of the Australian tariff rates. He has been followed by several other hon. members who have indicated .the extremely high tariff rates obtaining in Australia. It may be advisable at this point for me to refer briefly to the conditions which have brought that about, and I think in justice to Australia we ought to appreciate two or three matters to which I shall make reference. It is true that Australia has in recent years drastically increased her tariff rates. It is also true that Australia's exchange at the moment is under a serious discount. But why is it so? The reason is that Australia over a great number of years indulged, I might say, in rather expensive social legislation, which resulted in a very costly type of administration. This was followed by a very heavy expenditure, in proper-

Australian Trade Agreement
tion to her population, during the great war. I think I am correct in saying that the contribution which Australia made to the cause of the allies cost her perhaps more than that of almost any of the other dominions; at least in proportion to population it was a very heavy charge. Subsequent to the war, for these two reasons in the main, Australia found herself confronted with internal financial difficulties, and it was only in the last couple of years that her statesmen addressed themselves seriously to the correcting of those difficulties. Bringing their efforts down to date, they first of all increased the exchange rate. I may say that the Australian banks deal with this matter in a different manner from that followed by the Canadian, American or British banks. In Canada, United States and Britain, and, I think, in nearly all the other major countries, the exchange varies from day to day according to the necessities of the case-according to the demand for the money of one country in the market of the other, or the obligations to be met from time to time. So that exchange is constantly varying up and down in those markets. But under the Australian system of administering their banks, they arbitrarily fix the rate of exchange in a given period.
Now, under the circumstances to which I referred a moment ago, that is, the pressing necessity to correct their internal financial handicap, and the further necessity-which I overlooked-of paying their heavy interest charges abroad, both in New York and in London, Australia found it necessary to curb imports-that was her first step-in order to increase as far as possible the spread between exports and imports, thus giving her the goods or the financial value to pay her obligations abroad. To achieve this she imposed drastic increases in her tariff, and she raised her exchange, A year ago last January it was 3 per cent; it remained there for several months until she advanced it to 7 per cent; where it remained for several months and then she advanced to 9 per cent; where it remained until last January, when for a few days she raised it to 13 per cent, and later to 24 per cent, where it remains to-day. I am talking about the official exchange rates.
Is that imposed arbitrarily by Australia? Is it not imposed at ihe other end on Australia?

No, it is fixed by the Australian banks themselves, for the dual purpose of restricting the export of cash and the import of goods, with the idea of stimulating the exports in order to meet their obliga-

tions abroad. In addition to that Australia raised her tariff very substantially. Then the Australian authorities took one further step, for which I believe they deserve great credit. They cut all civil servant's salaries by 20 per cent; they cut all classes of pensions, including war pensions, 20 per cent; they cut down internal subventions 20 per cent; and they put into effect other drastic economies which have materially reduced their internal obligations. As a result of these efforts they have corrected their trade situation until for their fiscal year, ending, I think, last June, their exports exceeded their imports by $100,000,000. I cite that because those who are studying the situation closely believe that in this achievement alone one can perceive an early return of their exchange to par. I do not suggest that it will return to par rapidly, but I do believe that we shall see an improved condition in Australian exchange in the near future. I do wish to impress upon hon. members that the statesmen of Australia have seriously addressed themselves to the task of correcting the internal financial difficulties and uncertainties of the country. Therefore instead of criticizing the means which they have taken to achieve this end, I think we ought to recognize that they have taken a courageous and a bold stand in an effort to bring about this result.
Now, my hon. friend from North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) I am very sorry to observe is not in his seat, because I always prefer to direct my remarks to hon. members when they are in their seats, and I shall have to answer some of his points in his absence. Usually the hon. gentleman is perhaps one of the most fairminded and moderate debaters in the house, and I was a little disappointed in the attitude he took to-day in regard to this treaty. It is quite true he intimated that he was not opposed to the treaty, that he thought there were some good features about it, but then he spent the rest of his time citing individual items which he held up before the house as evidence of the ineffectiveness of the treaty, and that it would be indeed of little value to the country. In that respect I am fair to him in saying that he limited such remarks to the application of the British preference.
I am going to examine a few of the items he examined and a few more that he did not deal with; I am not going through the whole list. By the way, he was seeking to show that the Australian rates were so absurdly high that in any case the British preference meant nothing. "Why," he said, "the first item on this list carries a duty of 60 per

cent under the British preference, plus a surtax of 50 per cent of the duty." He did not say what the item was, but let us see what it is. He said, "You are not going to ship much goods under such a high rate; it means 90 per cent plus the primage tax and so on, so you need not expect to do much business under that rate." What is that item? It deals with corsets, an antiquated article of female attire. I do not know much about ladies' wear, but I am under the impression that the item of comets does not play quite so prominent a part as it did in my younger days, and I question whether, after the treaty has been in effect for a year or so, my hon. friend will find that the failure to jump the Australian hurdle of 90 per cent under this item of corsets is going to be a very great detriment to Canada.
I never mentioned corsets.

No, my hon. friend was
very careful not to mention them; he was a little shy and delicate. He said the first item on the list, and I am reading the first item.
I did not say that.

Yes, my hon. friend did
say so. Then he came along and made rather a pathetic appeal for his own riding. He said. "I have in my own riding a cordage factory," and he cited binder twine and yams.
I did not cite binder twine.
Yes, my hon. friend did.
I did not cite binder twine.

My hon. friend certainly
spoke of the item to which I am referring.

I spoke of cordage, but not
of binder twine.

not read the item correctly if he did not mention cordage. He said this item carried a duty of 40 per cent which, plus the 50 per cent surtax would be 00 per cent, and he said, "I cannot see much help for my riding under this item." I look across the page, and I find that under the old treaty it was 10 per cent, running up to 50 per cent in the case of some of the finer yams, while under the new treaty it is free and up to 40 per cent on some classes of yarns. In other words we are getting that item on the free list, but my hon. friend did 22110-258

not see that; he saw only the other item, which carries a very much higher rate of duty.
Then my hon. friend wept over refrigerating condensers and coils, which he said carried the iniquitously high rate of 45 per cent.

My hon. friend certainly
did. Does he say he did not refer to refrigerators?
No, I did not.

I cannot contradict my
hon. friend, but if he did not do so my memory is playing me false. At any rate, my hon. friend referred to another item below at 45 per cent, and the only one I see carrying that rate is the item dealing with refrigerating apparatus. Now 1 turn over the page, and while my hon. friend did not refer to these separate items he referred to certain agricultural items as not being under the British preference. I am going to refer to a number of items and give the rate which we now receive under the British preference, and I will also show what were the previous rates. The first item is handworked rakes and ploughs combined; handworked cultivators and handworked seed drills; under the old treaty the rate was 10 per cent and it is now free.
