Under the old treaty the rate was 30 per cent, while under the new treaty it is 20 per cent.



Australian Trade Agreement

I see
threshers are under the general tariff, while my hon. friend has just given them as free. How would that happen?

We come under the
British preference with regard to threshers. Discs for agricultural implements, formerly 10 per cent, now are free; grinding machines, formerly 10 per cent, now are free; unspecified metal working machinery, formerly 10 per cent, now is free. I may add that there is no surtax at all on any of the items I have just mentioned. Then there is an item covering boiler tubes which I hope will be of some value to Canada. Under the old treaty the rate was 10 per cent, and now they are free.
So I might go on; there are a larger number of these items, but the point I want to impress upon the house is that perhaps the most valuable provision of this treaty is that Australia extends to Canada the British preference, which previously we had only on four items. I pause to say this to my hon. friends:	When the discussions leading up to
this treaty were first undertaken there were two main points which had to be overcome. The first will answer the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) with regard to the dumping clause. Australia insisted that the application of the dumping clause should be waived on our part. On the other hand we insisted that the British preference should be extended to us in full. When that was ironed out we came to consider individual items now contained in the treaty, but those were the two main principles to be considered first. I regard them as of extreme importance. Let us look at the history of the dumping legislation. In 1925 Canada entered into a treaty-and I am not now going to blame my hon. friends opposite; I will say that Canada entered into a treaty with Australia, knowing perfectly well that there was such a thing as the Paterson scheme, and we put the rate on butter at one cent a pound. The treaty was passed in the autumn of 1925.
Is my hon. friend correct in his statement that the Paterson scheme was in operation in 1925?
Certainly.

I doubt it.
That is not my information.

Butter had been coming
into Canada quite freely, and I remember that my friend the late Hon. Mr. Boivin, Minister of Customs at that time, was
[Mr. Stevens.l
alarmed about the importations of butter and he imposed the dumping duty of 6 cents against Australia because of the Paterson scheme.

Yes, about February of
1926. The matter was discussed in January and February, and I have forgotten the exact date the dumping duty was imposed. Australia considered that this was more or less a shabby trick, shall I say, and they have never agreed that it was a fair imposition of the dumping clause. There was an element of unfairness in it, for this reason: All butter produced in Australia contributes 3 cents a pound to a pool, out of which was taken 6 cents per pound which was paid to the exporter of butter, so that really the exporter had already paid into the pool 3 cents a pound. Originally the amount involved was 9 cents per pound; that is, 3 cents was paid in and 6 cents was paid out. Later that was reduced to 6 cents, so that for a number of months, if not for the last year or two, there really has been a bonus of only 3 cents a pound. Recently-I have the date under my hand-that has been reduced to 5 cents a pound, so there is a bonus on Australian butter of cents a pound net, because prior to receiving the bonus the butter has contributed to the pool.
There is really no difference, except the reduction of one cent. They were doing the same thing before.

Yes, but it started at 9 cents, then dropped to 6 cents and now is 5 cents. That is the point I am making. I refer to that to emphasize the reasons why Australia requested the waiving of the dump. They never regarded it as a fair imposition and they insisted that it should be waived in the treaty. We waived it, but included in the treaty, by agreement with them, of course, after we had worked on it a considerable time, article IX, which we shall deal with in due course. Article IX is simply this:	that
either party to the agreement, if it is found that goods from the other country are being imported to the injury of any industry, may notify the exporting country accordingly and request the restriction of such exports. And it is assumed that the exporting country will immediately take action to restrict those exports. As regards Australia, the situation

Australian Trade Agreement
is very simple. They have export boards controlling butter, eggs, canned goods, meats and, indeed, most of the goods that may be affected by the treaty.
By what method can they restrict exports?

The export boards also control wine. In answer to the hon. gentleman's question, I am afraid I cannot go into details, but the method is this. They have export boards from which all exporters must get a licence before they can export goods.
We should have to have legislation to that effect?

We have not got that system. I am pointing out that Australia, whic-h affects us most, because we are the importing country, has the necessary machinery which it will put into operation the moment the need arises. Our experience with them during the past nine months gives us confidence in their fairness and we believe that they will actually put it into effect if necessary. But should they not do so, under Article IX we can, by our own action, remove the particular item from the treaty and it will fall automatically into the general tariff. The reason for that is this. We learned from the experience with the last treaty that an entire treaty may be wrecked by one item, and both countries agreed that this was an unwise position for either to find itself in. We therefore worked out Article IX to meet that difficulty, and: there is a genuine understanding, embodied in the treaty in definite language, and clearly understood by both, that an item may be removed without jeopardizing the rest of the treaty. And when the difficulty or dispute, or whatever you choose to call it, is adjusted, the item will go back into the treaty automatically by action of the government. We consider that an excellent method.
Reference has been made by one hon. member to the fact that we have lost our market in China for wheat, Australia being able to ship wheat to that country, under her depreciated currency, at much lower rates. Now, it is well sometimes to look at the facts. It is perfectly true that Australia this year has found a larger market in China for her wheat. It is lucky for us that she did, because it as lifted that much more wheat off the congested market of Europe. And we were delighted to see it. But what injury has that

And 1931 is the year in which we have been injured. These figures I submit indicate that no injury has been done to Canada-no material injury-in the Chinese market by Australia. On the contrary, the disposal of a large portion of Australian wheat in the far east has relieved the congestion of the European market, and personally I am delighted that Australia has found that eastern market this year, for her surplus wheat.
My hon, friend from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), in his usual manner, opened his remarks with a rather complimentary reference to the government and the treaty.
Is that my custom?
No, but I will tell the hon. gentleman what his custom is. I accept the correction. In opening his remarks he made some rather complimentary references to the government-
To the treaty.

-but, as is his custom, he spoiled the effect and value of these kindly and, I trust, just remarks by proceeding to a most unfair analysis of certain items of the treaty. Referring to eggs, he took good care to read into the record a letter from the Poultry and Egg Producers' Association of British Columbia. I received precisely the same letter, which I took care to answer, giving information which would remove the false impression they had. The hon. member knew -he admitted he knew-that the writer of that letter, a Mr. Wallace, was labouring under a misapprehension, not understanding all the facts. He had made the statements that appear in his letter without having the full information before 'him, or without troubling himself to look it up. Now what are the facts? I indicated them this afternoon. For the last six years eggs from Australia have been on the free list. During the last eight years, from 1923 to the present time, we have imported no eggs from Australia although they have been on the free list the whole of each year during that period. In this treaty we have restricted the free period to two months ' of the year, or one^sixth of the time under the old treaty; yet there are some who say that we are striking a dire blow at the very heart
*1062

Australian Trade Agreement
of the egg producing industry. The thing is so absurd that only a complete disregard of the facts or a complete ignorance of them would justify anyone in making any such statement. I was therefore veTy much surprised that my hon. friend from Comox-Albemi, who knew better, should read into the record the Letter in question. And the reason I interrupted him was that that letter appearing in his speech, which he would likely send out through the egg producing district of his riding, should not go without some challenge to the accuracy of the statements made by the hon. member, together with the letter as it was read.
The hon. gentleman then referred to butter, expressing apprehension of the effect of this treaty in the importation of butter into British Columbia in particular, and into Canada generally. I have already indicated the operation of the dumping clause. The facts regarding butter are these. Under the old treaty butter was one cent per pound, with the application of the dumping clause available to the government. Under the new treaty butter is five cents per pound but, instead of the application of the dumping clause, we have article IX, which provides a much more effective, expeditious and definite way in which to prevent any flooding of the market with butter. Bet me say as earnestly as I can that we are confident that Australia will not attempt to flood the Canadian market with butter. Australia takes the position that Canada during recent years has been a butter importing country, and she merely asks that if and when we import she may have a reasonable advantage in our market. We have given an advantage restricted to five cents per pound duty. During the session -we have been condemned because we put on a duty of more than four cents per pound. The hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) read a letter purporting to come from the national dairy council at Winnipeg wherein they declared that they did not want a duty of more than four cents per pound. He impressed this upon the attention of the house, and condemned the government because too high a rate was being put on. Australia has agreed to the rate of five cents per pound and we consider it reasonable and adequate, fortified as it is by article IX of the treaty.
This afternoon the hon. member for Cornox-Albemi attempted to get away with the assertion that he had been asked by the pulp industry to see that they were protected against any possible damage which might be done by this treaty. He modified that statement by saying that he had been asked to

speak on their behalf so that their interests might be protected. I told him this afternoon and I repeat now that he never presented that protest to the government. He is not a shy man, nor is he modest in the slightest degree- I question if he knows the meaning of the word-and if he had in his possession a request from the pulp industry of British Columbia asking for special consideration in the matter of preferences in connection with pulp, he never presented it to the government.

I said I had received the letter and I spoke absolutely correctly, but 1 did not say I had it with me. During the dinner recess I looked up this matter and, it being my custom to close up my files at the end of each session, I found that it was not on this year's file. Therefore it must have been last session and I must have presented it to the late government.

This afternoon my hon. friend was very positive that he had this letter. He was very certain that we were penalizing the pulp industry, he was very certain that we were neglecting this industry and that we were injuring it. I challenged him to show how we were injuring it, how we were penalizing it or how we were neglecting it, and he was narrowed down to asserting that he had the letter. Now he tells us that he has not the letter; it must have been a letter he received last year and passed on to hon. members opposite. I shall be very much interested in seeing that letter.
I will send it to my hon. friend as soon as I get home.
Does the minister think that the rate of Australian exchange will work to the advantage of that state in shipping goods to Canada?

I appreciate the sincerity of my hon. friend, but to discuss that question fully would necessitate one of those long debates which we have experienced in years gone by. I will answer the question, but I do not pretend that the answ'er will be complete. Undoubtedly some advantage would accrue to a country with a depreciated currency in the exchange of its goods with other countries, but it must be remembered that although it may not synchronize with the depreciated currency, the time will come when the cost of production rises correspondingly. It does not follow that that rise will be as rapid as the rate of depreciation; it never is, but it follows that the depreciation gradually is offset.

The advantage, then,
would be only temporary.

Quite so. It is a grave
question whether or not it is of any advantage to Australia, and I question whether it is of any advantage at all. We are undoubtedly concerned about it in a sympathetic way, but we believe the situation is being corrected and we look in the near future to a very rapid correction olf it. We certainly would not advise the holding up of this treaty because of the fact of depreciated currency. Furthermore, while I am not certain, I believe Australia has a provision in her tariff to prevent, and is recognizing the wisdom of preventing, the unfair competition of goods from countries with depreciated currencies. The other day a cargo of goods from Russia entered Sydney harbour, and the Australian government are, I believe, taking action to prevent those goods from entering into unfair competition with her own products. If that be so-and I believe it to be-certainly they will appreciate an appeal to them should it be proved that goods from Australia are entering Canada 'because of depreciated currency, in an unfair manner in competition with our goods.
Just a word in conclusion. Australia and Canada have similar tariff systems; they have a preferential, an intermediate and a general rate. Hitherto Australia has extended the British preference to the United Kingdom and New Zealand, and on four items, to Canada. She now extends the British preference to Canada, as the Prime Minister said this afternoon, on 415 items. True, on some of those items the British preferential rate will be high and will not permit of exchange, but this preference will give us perhaps two or three hundred items upon which we may enter the markets of Australia in competition with the United Kingdom. Furthermore, this is certain: whatever opportunity any countries may enjoy of entering the Australian market, we certainly enjoy the best. Last year Great Britain shipped goods into Australia to the extent of $277,000,000, and the preference netted Great Britain $35,000,000. That is what it is worth to Great Britain. We have

Australian Trade Agreement
now equal opportunity with Great Britain on all the range of goods that she sells to Australia. It may also be interesting to know that Australian imports are	divided	as follows:United Kingdom	
42	per	centUnited States	
23	per	centCanada	
3	per	centI invite the house	to	consider	the	possibilities for Canada under the new treaty with the British preference and special privileges that we have in the specified items. The United States have to their credit 23 per cent of the imports of Australia, while we have only 3 per cent, and now we have an opportunity in the Australian market on conditions surpassed by no other country, not even Great Britain.
The principle which has directed our efforts in connection with this treaty has been that o>f friendly cooperation between Australia and ourselves. We have at all times sought to work these things out in a fraternal spirit, if I might so put it. On every occasion we have been met with the most kindly response, and we anticipate the most hearty cooperation on their part just as we shall give it to them in the working out of the terms of the treaty.
Another point to which I might call attention is that so far as the items in the two schedules are concerned, we maintain the spread between the general tariff and the specified rates to Canada or to Australia, as the case may be. That is, however we may change our rate or they may change theirs, the spread between the general and the specified rates will be maintained.
Will my hon. friend explain that spread a little more fully?

In so far as the items
specified in the two schedules are concerned, the spread between the preferential rate extended by us to Australia or by Australia to us and the general rate will be maintained.

In the
Australian tariff?

And in ours-both ways.
I might mention also in connection with the treaty the question of inland freight rates. Under the Australian law determining the value for duty freight in the country of origin to the point of exit is included. To illustrate: Goods originating in Toronto, if shipped via Buffalo and San Francisco, would be dutiable in Australia at the cost of the goods plus the freight rate from Toronto to Niagara or Buffalo. If the goods perchance went by Vancouver, the rate of duty would be applied

on the cost of the goods plus the freight rate to Vancouver. The result was a tendency to ship the goods via United States ports, thus depriving Canadian ports of that business. That situation has been completely corrected. It was, I may say, in part corrected a year or two ago on the westward haul, but not on the haul eastward to Montreal, Halifax or St. John. Under the treaty this freight situation is completely corrected and the only freight charge to be added to the invoice price will be that to the nearest point of exit. From Toronto the nearest point will be Niagara or Buffalo.

Does that apply to
Canada?

It applies to both
countries. It is not important as applying to Australian goods coming into Canada, but in the case of Canadian goods entering Australia it is of great importance.

It does not apply to the
United States?

No. I have already given an explanation of article IX, and I shall not now repeat it.
We are asking the house to look upon this treaty as a genuine effort on the part of Canada as a whole, irrespective of party affiliation, or business interests, or locality, because we believe the treaty will be of advantage to the whole of Canada much more than is perhaps at the present time understood. We offer the treaty to the house in that spirit, that Canada as a whole has sought to work out and we believe we have succeeded in bringing before parliament a trade agreement with a sister dominion, which, while it may not be perfect or wholly satisfactory, is at least for the time being the best we could hope for and one that will be of advantage to Canada and, we trust also, of advantage to Australia.
That is not the case.

My hon.
friend will give me the information no doubt when we reach the committee stage.
All I wish to say is that that is not the case.

Australian Trade Agreement
taken is that the general tariff must increase by the same percentage as the preferential tariff. Speaking generally, therefore, we have no preference on agricultural implements, of which in former days we shipped considerable quantities to Australia, and we must go into the Australian market on the same footing as the United States. No hon. member opposite has said a single word about agricultural implements. To some degree at least we have been put out of that market through the sale of American machinery.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They make it themselves.

My right hon. friend will admit on account of our having no preference in the market the Americans did secure a fair share of the Australian business and to a considerable degree we lost out in the farm implement business. After all the main items in connection with which Canadian trade will profit the most, and the items I am very glad indeed to support-in fact I am glad to support the whole treaty-are timber and paper. My hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) was very critical of the action of the government which negotiated the treaty in 1925. He said if we had adopted the proposals of the late Mr. Robb we would not have had such a serious condition. True, there may have been some trouble, chiefly I believe in regard to raisins. At the time, however, the difficulties did not seem to be serious. Some members of that government felt that food products should be procured as cheaply as possible for the consumers of Canada, and to some extent we did oppose the proposal to increase the duties upon raisins. In the present instance my hon. friend is alarmed about wine; he fears that the industry in Canada will be interfered with by the importation of that commodity. Well, the minister has my sympathy. To introduce schedules in a treaty to please every part of Canada is a very difficult matter.
I am quite happy in that regard; there is no difficulty.

I am glad to know my hon. friend is happy, because the severest criticism he has received has come from my hon. friend across the way, who I believe intends to make further observations in committee.
After the argument of my hon. friend I cannot see that under the Paterson scheme, there has been any reduction, except the one cent which prevailed when the embargo was placed on the importation of Australian butter. The result was that Australian butter

did not come into Canada because the embargo kept it out. I am not complaining about that, nor would I complain very much if there was no duty upon Australian butter or if it had a free market in Canada. Hon. gentlemen opposite, of course, in order to carry out the theory that they advanced so strenuously during the recent campaign when they talked so much about the importation of New Zealand butter-and undoubtedly they did a great deal of damage to our government-felt it incumbent upon them to put a duty on butter, notwithstanding the fact that we told them time and again that owing to the 'Canadian product being shut out of the American market, we would within a period of a year or eighteen months at least be on an export basis; then it would not make very much difference whose butter was being imported into this country, for prices would be regulated in the markets in which we would have to sell our surplus. And that has happened to-day. Notwithstanding what hon. gentlemen opposite said throughout the rural constituencies, to-day they are forced to go back and admit that all the duty they have placed on butter does not help the price one iota so long as we are on an export basis. For a short time we did happen to be out of the export market, then a higher price for butter prevailed in Canada than in any other country, and New Zealand promptly diverted her Shipments from Britain to Canada. At once hon. gentlemen opposite took advantage of that exceptional condition to decry the Australian treaty and to make statements from one end of Canada to the other that were utterly untrue. In consequence they were able to secure the return of a greater number of their candidates than otherwise would have been possible. If it was butter that defeated the late government, and the same condition prevail again that we become a butter importing country-it will not happen, of course, because the United States will not admit our butter into their market again, and we shall be on an export basis when hon. gentlemen opposite appeal to the country four years hence-a duy of five cents a pound will not keep out imports of butter, particularly from Australia, for so long as the Paterson stabilization scheme is continued we shall have practically free imports of butter from Australia, and it would simply be a fitting retribution that hon. gentlemen opposite should slide out of office on the article on which they slid into office.
As the result of this treaty I hope our trade with Australia will be at least as great in volume as it was under the former treaty

Australian Trade Agreement
which hon. gentlemen opposite maligned so much. While I do not expect that that trade will be so much in favour of Canada, yet if we get our share of it, then it is all to the good. May I say to the government that so long as they secure business for Canada by treaties negotiated on a reasonable and equitable basis, then I am for them, for I have some sympathy with the statement made by the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) the other night. He mentioned a few things that are worth thinking about. For the last twenty years we have been improving our ports and our railway facilities, we have been spending huge sums of money upon our transportation systems, largely for the purpose of external trade, but the action of the government that he supports has put the greatest stumbling block in the way of our securing that trade and making payments on the vast expenditures so incurred. Every time there is any encouragement for Canada to increase her external trade, I am for it, so long as the trade treaty is upon reasonable and equitable terms for Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot allow this treaty to be adapted by the house without expressing my views. At the outset permit me to say that I approve of the treaty in almost all its terms. I have listened to the various speeches made this afternoon and to-night, and I have come to the conclusion that the introduction of this treaty has been a field day for British Columbia. The only reason I rise to enter a protest of any kind is that in some respects the treaty constitutes discrimination against the maritime provinces. I find item 51 (c) covers fish preserved in tins or other airtight vessels including the weight of liquid contents. This gives salmon a preference of 3 pence while crustaceans and other canned fish have a preference of only 1) pence. Now, every one knows that British Columbia is the largest producer of salmon in the world-

British Columbia does not
produce the crustaceans and other canned fish to which I have referred; these are produced in the maritime provinces and exported in large quantities. I wish to enter my protest on behalf of the fishermen of the maritime provinces against this way of treating that section of the Dominion. I have no fault

I am not
going to discuss the treaty at any length, Mr. Speaker, but I should like the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) to secure accurate information as to the present standing of the Paterson stabilization scheme. I have before me the November issue of the Journal of Agriculture of South Australia, and I desire to quote two paragraphs from a paper read by Mr. R. J. Finlayson at a conference of the Murray Lands Branches at Minardie. on October 1, 1929. Referring to the Paterson stabilization scheme he said:
The price of butter having advanced 3d. per pound, the farmer was immediately paid the enhanced price by his factory. Out of this 3d., however, he received only lid. per pound, the other lid. per pound being placed in a fund to provide the money necessary to pay a bounty of 3d. per pound (the difference between the two markets) on butter exported. The factory exporting is, therefore, no better or worse off than it was before, while the farmer, under this arrangement, was lid. per pound to the good.
Under the scheme all factories in the commonwealth have contracted to subscribe to the scheme, and to furnish each month to the secretaries of the various states duly certified returns, showing the amount of butter manufactured and the amount of money deducted from the farmers' payment. This money, which is forwarded to the secretaries, is placed in the bank to provide funds for the paying of bounties when butter is shipped.
After the plan had been tried out for two years, the committee found from experience gained that it could give further advantage to the supplier by increasing the levy and bounty, therefore on July 1st last-
I may say this is dated November 15, 1929.

the levy on the farmer was raised to lid. per pound and the bounty available for butter exported was raised to 4Jd-. per pound. The difference between the two prices was then 2fd. per pound, which amount the farmer receives by the extra price which he is paid for his butter.
It would seem that when this address was delivered the export bounty was equivalent to 9 cents per pound, but this evening I was informed by a gentleman who makes it his business to know these things that recently that amount has been reduced. He was not able to tell me exactly the amount, but was of the opinion that it was about 7) cents.

I hold in my hand a recent despatch which states that the Australian

Australian Trade Agreement
bounty on butter manufactured for export has been reduced from threepence to two-pence-halfpenny per pound, with effect from April 12.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Ait the moment hon. gentlemen should address themselves to the principle of the bill. A discussion of the individual items would be more in order in committee.

Perhaps the minister will be prepared to give a little more information when we discuss this measure in committee. I hope he will secure the fullest possible information on this point. I should like to know not only the bounty at the start, but what it was later and what it is at the present time. I should like also to be informed as to the time the Paterson scheme became effective. To-night it has been stated that this scheme was in operation when the former Australian treaty was negotiated. On that point I musit express a little doubt, because I am told the Paterson scheme came into effect in January, 1926, while the former treaty was made in 1925. Perhaps during the discussion in committee we will get these matters cleared up.

This will be the third occasion this session on which I have had the pleasure of supporting a government measure. The first was in connection with a very modest bill to amend the Root Vegetables Act, and I made what little contribution I thought necessary to assist the minister at that time. The second occasion was when I supported the duty on foreign oranges. That was a very unpopular thing to do, but nevertheless I think it will work out all right: That action was on all fours with the policy of the Liberal government in respect to bananas a few years ago, when the trade treaty with the West Indies was negotiated. Prior to that time 'bananas were nondutiable coming from all parts of the world, and the government of that day imposed a duty of 50 cents a stem on foreign bananas, leaving them free from the West Indies and other British dominions. That has worked out splendidly, and I think that the same result will come about in connection with oranges. I hope that within a short time we will be able to obtain sufficient oranges from the various parts of the British Empire to make us independent of foreign countries.
To-night I have much pleasure in supporting this bill, almost without reservation, though I intend to point out some defects and I hope my hon. friends will not take exception to what I have to say. I think they realize now

that they cannot buy a market in any country without paying for it. You cannot go into any store in this city and buy a hat, a pair of boots or anything else without having to pay some coin, and you cannot go to a sister dominion or to any other country and secure a market without not only giving something for it but also allowing them to export commodities which will compete with commodities produced in our own country.
I am supporting this bill for two particular reasons. It is the first evidence this session of returning trade sanity on the part of this administration, and I think it would be a terrible thing to not encourage that development in the future. The second reason is that this is the proper thing to do. I think from now on this parliament as a whole should support any bill which brings into being a treaty, after it has been threshed out with a sister dominion or whatever country it may be. When the government come down with an agreement and say, "This is the best that can be devised," we should give it a trial before condemning it. That is my honest opinion, as one who 'believes in the principle of interempire trade. Just imagine, Mr. Speaker, what would happen to this bill-because there are weak points in it, although to-night I am looking only for the strong points-if we ripped into it as hon. gentlemen opposite did with regard to the first Australian treaty from its very inception. Would that promote the cause of inter-empire .trade? I do not think it would. So I think from now on Canada should realize that any treaty brought down by any government should be given a fair measure of support before it is subjected to severe criticism by the. opposition, whatever opposition it may be. Give it a probationary trial; I think that is fair to any government, and it is the proper thing to do. I realize that to-day because of the utterly unfair criticism of the Conservative party in connection with the first Australian treaty. I do not want to say that with any soreness or bitterness; I speak as one who has experienced what it means to have a government measure very unfairly criticized and a treaty jeopardized. I always thought the old treaty was economically sound, but it was politically weak when exposed to the attack of an opposition which knew no limits to its criticism. So for those two reasons I support this bill.
Now I should like to refer briefly to some of the remarks of my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin). I have been asked once or twice this session, I think by my hon. friend from North Renfrew (Mr. Cotnam), why the government enacted the first treaty

Australian Trade Agreement
containing the tariff provision it did contain with regard to butter. It was stated from Melbourne, just after the late Mr. Robb left there in 1924, that we had the option of either increasing the general tariff or lowering the preference; we could do either so long as we gave Australia a 3 cent preference. Those are not my words; I say that is the statement which came from Melbourne. Assuming that to have been correct, we had the option of [DOT]either putting up the general tariff to 7 cents and leaving the preference at 4 cents or of putting the preference at 1 cent and leaving the general tariff at 4 cents. Whether we did rightly or wrongly, we took the latter course, which was in conformity with the general policy of the Liberal party in regard to preferences. We believe in creating preferences by lowering the British preference rather than by raising the general tariff. We raised the general tariff in connection with bdnanas as I have said, but that was an exceptional case.
As I say, rightly or wrongly we chose the. course which conformed to the general policy of the Libera! party with respect to preferences and lowered the British preferential rate instead of increasing the general rate. As a matter of fact I do not believe we could have passed the bill through this house if we had increased the general rate. As you know, Mr. Speaker, at that time the Progressive party were sixty-four or sixty-five strong and we had a majority of only one if everyone was in the house, so in a measure we were dependent upon that party. I think they advocated an even lower tariff then than the Liberal party, although we have some pretty low tariff men on this side of the house.
If my hon. friend will look up the records he will find that the Progressive party voted against that treaty.

I know they did last session, but not at that time on butter. And it was on a different question altogether-raisins, not butter. There is one matter with which I fancy the newer members are not familiar. The very first session after the late government came into power, the session of 1922, there was a real stand-up fight on the question of oleomargarine. The question was whether or not the prohibition of the manufacture and importation of oleomargarine should be restored. The government that had preceded that Liberal administration had continued the manufacture and free importation of oleomargarine, and when we came into power I myself took the position that we should revert to the pre-war condition of prohibition of this commodity.
The prohibition had been instituted by the Hon. Sydney Fisher, and it was abolished during the war, in 1917, as a war measure. I felt it was only fair all around, to the dairy industry particularly, that the prohibition should be restored, and the fight continued in 1922 and 1923, and almost into 1924. It seemed to me that anything in the way of a tariff that would artificially raise the price of butter at that time would once more start the agitation for the manufacture and importation again of oleomargarine. For four years after the Australian treaty was enacted butter in Montreal, No. 1 pasteurized, was selling at 40 cents per pound wholesale during the month of January. That would mean practically 50 cents per pound retail; and with butter selling at 50 cents per pound-indeed, it went higher, but we may take that as the average-and especially so soon after the struggle over the oleomargarine question, there was almost bound to be a renewed agitation for the removal of the prohibition against the manufacture and importation of that substitute. It was a severe fight, and I did not want the experience a second time. That was one . reason why I favoured a reduced preference to one cent per pound on butter rather than raise the general rate to 7 cents. I was of the opinion that anything that would raise the price of butter artificially would surely create an agitation for the importation and manufacture again of oleomargarine. Those were three reasons why it seemed advisable and expedient to do what we did at that time.
I will go further. The national dairy council came to the government on one or two occasions during 1926 and 1927 and interviewed Mr. Robb and myself with regard to the increasing of the duty to what it was before, that is, up to 4 cents. Mr. Robb invariably advised them to go to the tariff board. But the national dairy council had nothing in particular to submit to the board at that time. They had no evidence that New Zealand butter was injuriously competing with Canadian butter, and it was not until 1929 that they did appear before the board. By that time they felt they had a case, and as soon as they presented that case the matter was approved of by the tariff board and Mr. Dunning took the necessary steps to restore that duty, giving six months' notice. I suppose that had the dairy council worked up a case at an earlier date they would have gone to the board and obtained the same results. But as soon as they did go in 1929 they got the approval of the board and of

Australian Trade Agreement
the government as well. That is the story in a nutshell.
Under this new treaty the duty is one cent more than the dairy council asked for. What that 5 cents will mean I do not know. Now, I do not pretend to be very well versed in economics, but it was news to me that Australia could choose her exchange at will. I think there was a time when she could.
It is arbitrary.

It may have begun as an arbitrary depreciation of currency but 1 fear it is involuntary now. I remember well when our money had depreciated 13 or 17 cents. That was no act of Canada's. My own impression is that the exchange or any country depends upon the money markets of the world, and I have more than a suspicion that this is about the way it stands with Australia to-day, although I hope, as I am sure we all hope, that, they will soon be back to par. But in the meantime will the Australians not make as much on the present exchange as the duty represents? Will they not make 5 cents on the exchange? I think they will.
The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) this afternoon made a speech that had something in it, not only as regards butter but as regards every other commodity which Australia sells to Canada. I do not wish to make too much of this, but if the minister is relying on any deliberate act of Australia to restore her money to par to set this matter right, in order to give the 5 cents its full value, he is making a treaty based on pious hopes rather than on actual facts. I hope he will not resent my calling this to his attention. More than that, he has thrown away, rightly or wrongly, any power to dicker on the basis of the dumping duty.
Oh no.

After three months' notice, of course. That was always there. I myself got the opinion of the Deputy Minister of Justice that we could have abandoned any one feature of the act ourselves by giving six months' notice. And if I remember rightly that was what Mr. Dunning did in regard to New Zealand.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It was the whole treaty.

That may be; I
was not here at the time. However, I had the opinion of the Deputy Minister of Justice that the duty on butter could have been dealt with separately if we had thought it advisable to do that, by giving the usual six months' notice. At any rate, I do not believe that the national dairy council, when they supported 
the proposal for 4 cents rather than 8 cents on Antipodean butter, took into consideration the question of depreciated currency. And I must admit that when I discussed the matter earlier in the session I did not take it into consideration either. But I know what the effect is. I shipped grass seed into the United States for many years, at a time when our currency was depreciated, and I was surprised when I deposited in my local bank the cheque I got from the American side for my carload of grass seed to find that for every 8100 I had been expecting I received 1113 Canadian dollars. That was the first time in my life I was so agreeably surprised by a similar cause. I knew, of course, that if I spent that money in a foreign country I should lose as much as I had gained. I knew in a general way that a depreciated currency enabled you to sell your commodities in another country to better advantage than you could when your own money was at par. So much for that.
May I now briefly refer to eggs. I always thought that two weaknesses had developed under the old treaty; I will make that admission. Those weaknesses were not inherent in the treaty at the beginning but they appeared later. I refer to the matter of eggs and onions. I do not believe that anyone ever expected that very many eggs would be shipped either way. Under the old treaty eggs from Australia were free. I am not sure at what rate eggs were going into New Zealand and Australia from Canada under the British preference, but if I remember rightly the rate into New Zealand was 8 cents and into Australia 17 cents. But that did not matter much so long as no eggs were moving either way. And the fact is that practically no eggs came from Australia to Vancouver or elsewhere in Canada. But some trade was worked up once or twice when the markets for eggs were quite low in eastern Canada; Vancouver tried to ship to Australia. Their eggs, I believe, had to climb over a wall of 10 or 17 cents; I do not remember exactly which. Perhaps my hon. friend can tell me what it was under the old treaty. What is the duty on eggs going into Australia under the new treaty? Are they not 10 cents into Australia?
I think they are 10 cents.
Sixpence.
I am not certain.

It seems strange
that Canadian eggs can go over the Pacific waters to Australia in fair condition while Australian eggs cannot acceptably come to Canada. If the hon. Minister of National

The government I repeat has had the experience of five or six years and if they could not make an improvement on the old treaty they would not amount to very much. I hope we will learn, as an opposition, from hon. members opposite, how not to treat a new treaty with a sister dominion. Perhaps that will be one benefit which will come out of this treaty.
I do not think it would be quite fair to judge the trade results of the new treaty by the old. It is not fair to compare the last four or five wonderful years of development under the old treaty with the next four or five possible sub-normal years under the new. I do not know how long I will have to keep myself under discipline and refrain from criticizing this new treaty. Conditions probably will not be sufficiently normal for at least two years, but I do not know whether I will have sufficient grace to keep quiet about this treaty and give it a fair trial for that length of time, but I will try.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to make but a few general observations on the principle of this bill. In that this treaty represents an earnest and honest endeavour on the part of the government to improve the trade relations of Canada with our sister dominion, I think hon. members generally thoroughly approve

Australian Trade Agreement
of it. My own opinion is that the treaty is a fair one for Australia and a useful one for Canada. It has every promise of bringing to us that which we need and of providing an extension of markets for many of our products, particularly those of our fisheries, our lumbering and paper industries, and certain of our manufacturing industries. The principle of the treaty is similar to that of the treaty which was put into force by the former government.
So far as Canada is concerned, there are two main points in the treaty. First, we give Australia an advantage in our markets for her agricultural products, and, second, we give Australia a preference on some of her fruit exports. As to the latter, we give a preference by increasing the duty against other countries, notably the United States, and in so doing we extend the principle made operative by the former treaty in respect to raisins and apply it to other fruit, such as oranges.
On behalf of agriculture I must voice a protest. The inevitable outcome of a treaty with a dominion such as Australia is that any advantage given to certain classes of industry in this country must be paid for. Unfortunately, owing to the fact that Australia is not a manufacturing country, that preference must be paid for by agriculture, not by a reduction of duty but by the opening of our doors to the agricultural products of Australia. I am not taking violent objection to that. Anything we get that is worth while for Canada as a whole must be paid for by some sacrifice on our part. It is unfortunate of course that invariably such sacrifices must be made by agriculture; to what extent this will affect agriculture time alone will show. I am not of opinion that Australian butter, eggs or meat will at the present time at least, enter Canada in any large quantities to displace the Canadian article. As regards butter-and I am speaking of butter because it was perhaps the outstanding issue of the last treaty, particularly as it related to its extension to . New Zealand-the situation has completly changed since that time. We were then in a position to take advantage of a domestic market and to receive a higher price for our butter in this country than the world market would justify. At the present time we are, and I would expect for some time to come we shall be, on an export basis. Therefore I doubt very much that there will be any large imports of Australian butter, and also whether any imports there may be will have any effect on the price under present conditions.

Speaking generally, then, we have negotiated a treaty favourable to this country; it is favourable particularly to certain industries, and to the extent that it is paid for by any corresponding sacrifice within this country, it is paid for by agriculture. Time alone will show the extent to which agriculture may have to pay for it. But on the face of the treaty as it stands to-day, and leaving out two factors which I shall mention briefly in a moment, I think it is a fair treaty which can be supported. We can leave it to time to show whether it will work out to the ultimate advantage of all. I certainly agree with the ex-Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) that it would be foolish, unjustifiable, for us to attempt at this stage to destroy the treaty.
The two factors to which I allude, and the full significance of which is at this stage unknown, are the question of exchange and the question of the Paterson bonus scheme upon export butter. It is obvious, by the action of the Australian bankers as described by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), that, whatever arguments may be adduced in opposition, they at least believe that this discount on their exchange works to the advantage of their exports, making it easier for them to place their exports in other countries. The same thing is clear from our own experience when our currency was at a discount in the United States and when we could ship cattle into that country and pay the duty through the disparity in exchange. How long this situation will last and to what extent it will affect us, time again alone will show. At the moment, however, it is apparent to everyone that the disparity in exchange alone will at least equal the protection which remains to domestic as compared with Australian butter, and the same thing applies to Australian meat, eggs and any other article coming from that dominion. In the same way and to the same degree Canadian exporters, those who, it is expected, and we hope, will be benefited by this treaty, will be placed at some disadvantage if the expressed object of the Australian bankers is fulfilled, namely, to increase exports and to discourage imports, to make it easy for them to sell and to make it difficult for us to sell in return. While this fact is obvious, the extent to which it will operate and the time over which it will extend are unknown quantities.
As regards the Paterson bonus scheme, there is a levy of two and a half cents a pound in our own money and a bonus of five cents a pound. This means a net bonus of two and

Australian Trade Agreement
a half cents a pound, because the export butter pays one-half of the bonus it receives. So we have to add to the other advantage another two and a half cents a pound. Again, no one knows the extent to which that will work, or to what degree it will place a disadvantage on our farmers. So long as we are on an export basis, may I repeat I doubt whether it will make much difference, but the moment we slip below an export basis, then we shall be able to see exactly what the result will be.
I repeat that I am sure no hon. member in our part of the house would feel justified in placing obstacles in the way of a treaty which in its general terms is designed to nullify part of the policy of the present government; which is designed to encourage international trade and the interchange of commodities between this Dominion and Australia. So far as the disadvantage may be placed upon any individual product of the Canadian farmer or manufacturer, we may again look to article IX if that disadvantage becomes obvious and if the unfairness becomes equally so. It is certainly to the advantage of the government to see that this treaty operates to the benefit of Canada and does as little harm as possible to any Canadian citizen. Undoubtedly for the sake of their own reputation, apart from their honest desire to serve Canada, they will see that such is the case. We shall trust, then, that under article IX they will be able to meet any unexpected and untoward situation which may arise, and in the meantime, reserving any further remarks until the bill is in committee, we can assure the minister of our qualified and, in view of the principle which I have already outlined, somewhat critical support.

I should like to say a

Under the old legislation the duty charged against butter entering Canada from Australia was one cent per pound. At that time the Minister of National Revenue applied the dump against Australia. With six cents added to the one cent duty, the duty against butter from Australia was raised to seven cents a pound. Under the present schedule the dump against butter is not to be applied under any consideration, and the duty of five cents per pound is in force. The result is that the duty against butter is two cents less than it was under the late administration.

My hon. friend is not
quite correct. I have already explained that Australia always felt more or less hurt concerning the action of Canada in applying the dump. She felt that under the terms of the old treaty such action should not have been taken, and the matter of the dump became one of the principle points of adjustment between the two countries. Through the adoption of article IX an adjustment was reached and while it is clearly understood that section 6 of the Customs Tariff,- the dumping clause, will not be applied, article IX will take its place. Instead of one cent per pound against butter we have a definite duty of five cents. Should Australian butter enter Canada in a manner which would prejudicially affect the interests of dairymen, notice is given to that effect. I may say that this article has been in operation, although it has not existed in the form of a contract. Australia however has voluntarily complied with requests to curb exports to this country when it was felt that such exports would be injurious to Canadian interests. Under the article such a curb becomes obligatory. If measures to remedy the conditions complained of are not put into effect by the exporting country within three months, the notice is made effective by action of the importing country. We believe article IX will be quite effective if not more effective than the dump, and will remove the stigma of applying a dumping duty.

Under our general tariff
sugar up to 98 degrees carries a steadily increasing ratio of duty. From 98 to 99 degrees it jumps, instead of at about one cent per pound, from about 30 cents to 35 cents. There is a little higher degree of refining in the first process. As hon. gentlemen know, there are two general processes, the milling and the refining. In most of the countries exporting sugar to Canada the sugar is purified to 96 degrees, and some of it to 97 and 98 degrees. One colony, Mauritius, I think, purifies it up to 99 degrees, but when Australia installed their milling system, which merely deals with the raw cane, and established their refineries they did so on the basis of the first process carrying the purification up to about 99 degrees-I am not certain whether it is 98j or 99 degrees, but for our purposes they are about the same. So in order to give Australia a portion of our Canadian market for what is known as raw sugar we increased the classification from 98 to 99 degrees, which permits the sugar from Australia to enter our market for refining purposes.
The hon. member for South Huron is mistaken, and I do not criticize him for it because these are technical matters. I do not pretend to be an expert in them, but I have given a good deal of study to this question during the past few months, and I can assure the hon. gentleman that there is no bonu3 at all going to the refineries under this item They have to pay the same ratio of increase for this added degree as they pay down the whole list; it increases at a steady ratio, and sugar of 99 degrees polarization is not a refined sugar. in our trade with Australia is that much of our business with them is bulk business- paper, lumber, and heavyweight cargoes- while much of their business with us is more or less of confined space, like dried fruits, and so on. tion for Canadian industry. I have no special brief for anyone in that business, but the committee will agree that so long as it is a legal commodity which is produced in this country it is at least as much entitled to protection as any other commodity. Brandy coming from Australia is allowed in at a duty of $8 per gallon. Brandy is produced in Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Where? I am told not.

I understand it is. However, I will read a telegram which I have received and I shall be glad to get an adequate reply; because, so far as I can see, the protest is a just one. Australian brandy can. come under this treaty at $8 peT gallon. Canadian-produced brandy pays to the government an excise duty of $9 a gallon, so that it has not an equal opportunity. The two are not even on an equal basis, the Australian producer actually having an advantage over the home producer of $1 per gallon.
Where is brandy produced in Canada?
You are doing the same thing under the French treaty at this moment.
That may be, but two wrongs do not make a right.
I agree with you.

My hon, friend has protested against the reduced duty on Australian wines; but so far as wines are concerned the Canadian producer has at least a little protection left. The Canadian producer of brandy, if there are any producers,-
No.

-on the other hand, is discriminated against. Perhaps I had better read the telegram I have received. I repeat, I have no brief for them, but if there are legitimate producers of brandy in Canada they have a right to protection under the principles laid down by my right hon. friend. I have no doubt he has also received this telegram. It reads:
Understand Australian treaty allows entry into Canada of Australian brandy at eight dollars per gallon. At present Canadian excise

duty on spirits is nine dollars per proof gallon so that a substantial preference is given to importers over the domestic manufacturer who employs Canadian labour not only directly but indirectly through many other industries. Canadian distillers are also large users of Canadian rye and barley. It is obviously unfair that this important Canadian industry which has thousands of shareholders should thus be discriminated against and we respectfully ask that appropriate steps be taken _ to remove the disadvantage placed on Canadian spirits.
It is signed by ten distillers. I need not read the names.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It might be just as well.

They are: Hiram Walker & Sons, Limited; Distillers Corporation,Limited; Jos. E. Seagram & Sons, Limited; Gooderham & Worts, Limited; Canadian Industrial Alcohol Company, Limited; Consolidated Distilleries, Limited; Wiser's Distillery, Limited; B.C. Distillery Co., Limited; United Distillers, Limited; Pioneer Distillers, Limited.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I suggested that my hon. friend should read the names for this reason. I say to him here and now that not one of those firms produces a single gallon of brandy.
If they do not, I have nothing to say.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have under my hand from one of the largest of the firms who have signed the telegram-I need not mention the name-a letter in which the statement is made:
Answering your inquiry, would say no brandy is manufactured in Canada.
I wish to make rthat perfectly clear. And as the hon. gentleman has said that he has nothing further to say if there are no producers of brandy in Canada, it is not necessary that I should take up the time of the committee further.
If it is the fact that no brandy is produced in Canada, I have nothing to say.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is the fact.

While there is no brandy produced in Canada, the preference given to brandy from Australia, as against the S9 per gallon excise on Canadian spirits, makes brandy cheaper and it therefore comes into competition with whiskies and other spirits manufactured in this country. That is why they are protesting. It will be observed that in the telegram they say "Canadian spirits;" they do not say brandy. Brandy having a $1

preference over the Canadian excise of 89 per gallon, it is so cheap as to come into competition with all Canadian spirits.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
In view of the observations of my hon. friend from Gloucester (Mr. Veniot), perhaps I might add this. My hon. friend from North Waterloo will recall that this afternoon, when moving the second reading of the bill, I explained that it was our purpose to prefer, under equal conditions, the British dominions to foreign countries. This brandy comes into competition with French brandy, and we could not apply a higher rate than $8 because the French treaty stands in the way. This treaty was made by my hon. friends and fixed the duty at that rate. If Australian brandy is to compete in this country with French brandy, obviously the same rate or less had to be applied. France is something like three thousand miles away from this country while Australia is over twice that distance.
Schedule A agreed to.
On schedule B.

I would like to have an
explanation of what appears to me to be a discrimination against fish packed in the maritime provinces.

There certainly was no
intention to discriminate against the maritime provinces. It must be recognized that Australia fixed the rates in this schedule.
Why would they determine to give such a high preference to salmon? Surely the minister should have discussed the other fish.

We not only thought of
it but this was one of the important items which were under negotiation.

It is a good thing for
British Columbia but it would appear to be discrimination against the maritimes.

She does not can other
kinds of fish.
Private Bills
Oh yes, they can some.

Not the type of fish we
send to Australia. The largest sardine canning factory in the world is located in New Brunswick, and this country has always held the Australian market for sardines. The preference on sardines has not been increased while the preference on salmon has been doubled.

The duty on crustaceans is
five cents per pound British Preferential and eight cents per pound general tariff. That is a three cents per pound preference on crustaceans.

And six cents per pound
on salmon.
Yes, that is right.

Does the minister think
that is a fair deal?

It is the best we could,
do.

I want to see this treaty'
go through, but I want to see fair play given to the people of the maritime provinces. I suggest to the minister that between now and the next session he take up this matter with the Australian authorities and see if we cannot obtain the same preference as applies to salmon.
We shall be glad to discuss it with Australia.

Is it not a
fact that this agreement has to pass in its entirety and that no matter how long we continue the discussion, there is no possibility of
amending it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is quite right.
Schedule B agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

Mr. Speaker, by leave of the house I desire to move, seconded by the hon. member for West Algoma (Mr. Simpson):
That the following bills of the Senate, namely: Bill No. 137, for the relief of Pearl Whelan and Bill No. 138, for the relief of truce Raymond Diamond, be now read a first and a second time and referred to the select standing committee on miscellaneous private bills.

Motion agreed to.
